witnesses.name: Vusimuzi Cat Matlala
witnesses.role_as_described: Implicated person continuing cross-examination on his relationships with Hangwani Morgan Maumela, Suleiman Carrim, Jotham Msibi and Mr Motsumi, and on the SAPS Medicare24 Tshwane health-risk-management contract

summary: Mr Matlala continued his cross-examination by Advocate Sello SC on his supplementary statement, beginning with a dispute over whether NPA/NDPP correspondence (CJC442) showed he was under investigation over recordings of his December 2024 and May 2025 interrogations; the Chairperson ruled the letter did not establish this and required specificity before any privilege could be claimed. The Commission then examined an SIU Special Tribunal freezing order (Annexure A) that listed companies linked to Matlala, with the Chairperson and Commissioners Baloyi and Khumalo finding it did not show Matlala himself was under investigation. Matlala was pressed at length on a 'revolving fund' arrangement with Hangwani Morgan Maumela for supplying medical consumables to the Gauteng Department of Health via a 'main supplier' (identified as Telox), and on WhatsApp chats with the late Jotham Msibi showing shared payment notifications (naming Agrippa Khoza and referencing Maumela), an aborted aircraft purchase, and a VIP-lounge business proposal, which Commissioners said indicated a closer relationship than the 'mere service provider' account he had first given. In the afternoon, Matlala described a R5 million loan (later acknowledged by debt, not a loan agreement) from businessman Mr Motsumi to his company Medicare24 Tshwane, and a separate unrealised R20 million investment proposal tied to funding the SAPS Medicare24 contract, before evidence leaders moved to a letter of demand for non-performance on that SAPS contract, where Matlala repeatedly declined to answer questions citing his pending criminal trial.

rulings.description: The Chairperson ruled that Annexure CJC442 (the DPP/NPA letter) does not show Mr Matlala is under investigation or a suspect in respect of the December 2024/May 2025 recordings, and that Ms Sello could proceed to question him on the recordings; any assertion of privilege must specify the crime and basis, per paragraph 109 of the Constitutional Court's Jafta judgment.

The Chairperson and Commissioners Baloyi and Khumalo ruled that the SIU Special Tribunal freezing order (with Annexure A listing Matlala's companies) does not indicate Matlala himself is under investigation, since the order concerns the named respondents' beneficial interests in other people's entities, not those entities being investigated.

Commissioner Baloyi ruled that, since Matlala accepted he had never been approached by any investigator and the SIU document he relied on did not establish suspect status, he was required to answer the Regulation 10.6 questions about his relationships with Mr Maumela and Mr Carrim.

The Chairperson found that nothing in Matlala's account of the Maumela 'revolving fund' arrangement self-evidently disclosed criminality, and that Matlala could not assert privilege merely by saying an unspecified investigation might exist; he was required to identify a specific offence.

On Ms van den Heever's objection concerning Mr Matlala's constitutional/section 35 fair trial rights, the Chairperson ruled that any invocation of such rights must be specific to a particular question and document, not raised as a blanket objection; he pressed Ms van den Heever to substantiate the point immediately rather than deferring to the next day.
Commissioner Baloyi ruled that further submissions/legal argument on section 35 rights be deferred so evidence-leading with Mr Matlala could continue before the 4pm adjournment.

witnesses.role_as_described: Continuing witness under subpoena, giving supplementary testimony and undergoing questioning on his relationships with senior police officials and others; separately an accused/suspect in the Medicare tender criminal trial and in a separate Pretoria criminal matter

summary: The sitting day opened with an extended procedural dispute over Mr Matlala's legal team's request to postpone argument of his constitutional-rights application (seeking broad immunity from questioning on self-incrimination grounds) until the next day; the Chairperson refused the postponement and, after Matlala's team briefly threatened to withdraw from the brief, ruled the Commission would proceed. Matlala's team then elected to continue representing him, with Matlala reserving his right to claim privilege question-by-question rather than pursuing blanket immunity. The remainder of the day was taken up with Matlala reading supplementary responses into the record concerning his relationships with numerous individuals listed in the Commission's Regulation 10.6 notice, and extensive questioning - much of it focused on his previously undisclosed relationship with Lieutenant General Shadrack Sibiya and the disappearance of Mr Jerry Boshoga - during which Matlala repeatedly invoked self-incrimination and referenced an ongoing, unspecified state investigation and a section 204 affidavit he argued remained privileged. The hearing adjourned at 17:58 to resume the next morning.

rulings.description: Refused Mr Matlala's legal team's application to postpone argument of his constitutional-rights/self-incrimination application until the following day; directed that the application be argued at 12 midday that day.
Formal ruling that, having considered the submissions, the Commission would go ahead and hear Mr Matlala's application rather than granting a further postponement.

Ruled that a document Mr Matlala produced that morning (said to show he is a suspect in a matter involving Mr Hangwani Morgan Maumela) was not shown to be privileged and should be shared with the Evidence Leaders that same afternoon.

Held that Mr Matlala could not refuse to answer a question about a civil application he brought for the return of seized personal property on the basis that answering would disclose his defence strategy in a separate criminal matter, finding no cogent link and no accepted legal basis for that objection.

exhibits.description: Document produced by Mr Matlala on the morning of the sitting, said by him to show he is a suspect (money laundering) in a matter involving Mr Hangwani Morgan Maumela; ordered to be shared with the Evidence Leaders that afternoon.

summary: The sitting opened with Fadiel Adams MP correcting two points of his prior testimony -- how he travelled to Orlando Police Station and the basis for his view that his case dockets had been sabotaged -- before evidence leader Adv Segeels-Ncube took him through his section 27 affidavit and the discrepancy over whether it mentioned the PKTT and a forklift; Adams was excused around midday. In the afternoon Lieutenant Colonel Deenadayalan Govender, head of the KZN PKTT, was sworn in and began testifying that in mid-to-late August 2026 he was repeatedly approached by an intermediary known as Mavuso, who arranged calls in which a man Govender identified by voice as Police Minister Senzo Mchunu urged him to tell the Commission he was acting on instructions from Lieutenant General Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi in relation to police shootings. Excerpts of audio recordings and transcripts (marked DG1-DG3, with further items DG4-DG6) of these calls and a related meeting were played, and the Commission made a procedural ruling setting a timeline for Govender's pending in-camera application covering separate, more sensitive evidence (including regarding a Mr Clive Naicker) to be resumed on 31 August 2026.

summary: The Commission continued the testimony of MP Fadiel Adams, focusing on documents he says he received anonymously (relating to the forklift procurement matter and General Madondo), his reliance on the late General Andre Lincoln as an information source, and the circumstances of him laying criminal charges at Orlando and Langlaagte police stations in Gauteng after first laying charges in Cape Town. Evidence leaders and Commissioners pressed Adams on inconsistencies, including his 1 November 2024 email to the Minister of Police alleging Gauteng dockets had already been intercepted (which he conceded was poorly worded and not strictly accurate), his non-disclosure of General Lincoln and of a Portfolio Committee approach to earlier bodies (Ad Hoc Committee, IGI, IDAC), and his admitted 'brush off' of SAPS Inspectorate investigator Colonel Phillips despite a same-day WhatsApp record showing Phillips explained the purpose of his call. The Commission also addressed logistics around a 2.5-hour recording of Adams' 6 January 2025 IDAC consultation, which Adams was given time to listen to during breaks so he could identify clips to play in evidence; a separate matter concerning subpoenaed JMPD officer Mr Johannes Mogatle was postponed to a date to be determined, with a directive that his statement be filed by the next day.

rulings.description: JMPD officer Mr Johannes Mogatle's testimony postponed to a date to be determined; directed to file his statement by the following day.

Arrangement confirmed for Mr Adams to listen to the full 2.5-hour recording of his 6 January 2025 IDAC consultation during tea and lunch adjournments, with agreed clips to be played in evidence; extracts must relate only to matters before the Commission.
Chairperson accepted evidence leader's proposal that any portion of the recording not finished by lunch would still be played from where Adams had reached, so cross-examination could continue.

Hearing adjourned mid-afternoon and postponed to 21 August 2026 at 9:30, with agreement that Adams' evidence would be completed by tea time the next day and that Adams would hand over details of his criminal case against IDAC officials before the following day's session.

summary: Fadiel Adams MP, sworn in, resumed testimony in the IDAC stream of the Commission, led by Adv Segeels-Ncube. The Chairperson first confronted Adams with a correspondence bundle showing he had received and responded to a Rule 3 notice in October 2025, contradicting his 11 August 2026 evidence that he only became aware of Commission communication three months earlier; Adams conceded the earlier statement was untruthful and apologised. Adams then took the Commission through large parts of his written statement, covering his background, his role as a Cape Town councillor and MP, his complaints about the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) budget, his concerns about Crime Intelligence, his account of anonymous documents (including a polygraph document concerning General Madondo and forklift/'heister' procurement records) left under his parliamentary office door in October 2024 that led to his section 27 referral to IDAC, his criticism of IDAC's conduct and members, and the events surrounding his own arrest and pending criminal case linked to the PKTT. Commissioners Baloyi SC and Khumalo SC also questioned him, including on the chronology of dockets he alleges disappeared after he laid complaints, and the day was adjourned for the evening with Adams' testimony to continue the next day.

summary: With Mr Matlala's testimony postponed and no substitute witness available, evidence leader Adv Chaskalson SC used the day to present WhatsApp chat extracts from the phone of the late Mr Jothan Msibi and related police witnesses. The evidence traced an alleged scheme in which Sergeant Fannie Nkosi fraudulently signed and stamped a letter on SAPS letterhead to enable a Czech company, Invasys, to demonstrate IMSI-catcher 'grabber' and jamming technology, ostensibly to SAPS but actually with a view to selling it to the Kingdom of Eswatini. Further chat extracts linked Mr Msibi to Carnilinx (recovery of stolen tobacco stock and firearms), to an alleged rigged tender at the City of Ekurhuleni benefiting Kamprock (Pty) Ltd, to a joint venture involving Mr Karim's Ziggy Investments and Transnational Coaches in subsidised bus contracts, and to an unlicensed-looking dagga (cannabis) cultivation operation at Jack Frost Pharmaceuticals in Germiston. Commissioners repeatedly raised concerns about the legality of grabbers and jammers in private hands and about the implications of a SAPS stamp being used to authorise an international transaction.

summary: On Day 160 the Commission began the scheduled testimony of Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala, who was sworn in and had his 10.6 statement read into the record after his counsel, Adv van den Heever SC, raised concerns about voluminous bundles (over 2,000 pages) served only the previous afternoon. Matlala repeatedly invoked the right against self-incrimination on questions touching his pending criminal charges over the Medicare24 SAPS tender, declining to address 13 named SAPS officials he described as co-accused and several other individuals listed in Annexure A of the 10.6 notice, while confirming or denying relationships with a number of others, including a detailed account of alleged extortion by Brown Mogotsi purportedly linked to former Minister Bheki Cele and Minister Senzo Mchunu. The Chairperson repeatedly pressed Matlala and his counsel to distinguish factual answers from assertions of privilege, and at the end of the day set a strict timetable for a supplementary affidavit and an application on points in limine, postponing continuation of Matlala's testimony to 24-25 August 2026.

rulings.description: Supplementary affidavit and application on points in limine to be filed by Mr Matlala by 10:00 on 21 August 2026; Evidence Leaders' answering affidavit by 10:00 on 22 August 2026; Matlala's replying affidavit and heads of argument by 18:00 on 22 August 2026, and Evidence Leaders' heads of argument by 18:00 the same day; continuation of Mr Matlala's testimony postponed to 24 and 25 August 2026, to continue on 26 August 2026 if not finalised, with no slippage on filing dates permitted.

summary: The morning session dealt with the non-appearance of witness Suliman Carrim, who again failed to testify despite a 29 July ruling requiring either his appearance or an independent medical report; after lengthy argument between Adv Hassim SC (for the Evidence Leaders) and Adv Premhid (for Carrim) on audi rights, voluntariness and the adequacy of the late medical report, the Chairperson announced the Commission would direct its Secretary, Dr Vukuza, to lay a criminal charge against Carrim rather than merely recommend one. witnesses.name: Ashley Lynton Houston
witnesses.role_as_described: Retired SAPS Captain (38 years' service, Durban); first police responder to reach the Morningside flat shooting scene on 1 April 2023

summary: Gregory Loftus, father of the late Bevan Loftus, testified that his son was killed along with four other men by a SAPS team at a Morningside, Durban flat on 1 April 2023, and that the operation was in fact an execution orchestrated at the instance of tow-truck rival Clive Naicker and carried out under Captain Deena Govender. Loftus described having deposed to an interdict application the day before the shooting seeking to stop Govender and SAPS from killing his son, and read extensively from his statement covering his son's employment, prior arrests, and the events leading up to the shooting. Later in the day, retired Captain Ashley Houston, the first police officer to reach the scene, testified that he found and identified two of the five deceased men, and, drawing on his firearms and tactical experience, said the police account of a mutual shootout in the confined flat was tactically improbable given the volume of rounds fired without any responding officer being hit. The hearing was adjourned for several tea breaks during the day and postponed to 14 August 2026, with Captain Houston's evidence to continue.

witnesses.name: Len John
witnesses.role_as_described: Deputy Director for Investigations, Independent Police Investigative Directorate (IPID), KwaZulu-Natal

summary: John gave evidence on alleged unlawful killings by SAPS task teams in KwaZulu-Natal and on alleged collusion between officers and tow-truck operators linked to drug trafficking and turf disputes. He told the commission that 149 people had died in 77 incidents involving task team operations between April 2023 and May 2026. He described a pattern in which operations took place late at night, officers covered their faces, and all suspects present were killed, and said the firearms recovered were often inconsistent with the cash-in-transit robbery profile attributed to those killed. He alleged that some officers received payments from tow-truck operators and drug gang figures for protection and for targeted killings, and connected the April 2023 killing of Bevan Loftus to an alleged offer of R2.5-million to Lieutenant-Colonel Deena Govender by a rival operator. Evidence was also heard about R2.3-million allegedly deposited into the accounts of a police officer and his wife.

witnesses.role_as_described: Head of Investigations and Operations, Investigating Directorate Against Corruption (IDAC)

summary: Sesoko gave evidence about IDAC's internal case selection processes and about changes to his own authority. He told the commission that after returning to work in January 2026, following his kidnapping in November 2025, he found structural changes had been made without explanation, including the loss of a committee chairmanship and of supervisory responsibility over chief investigators. He said certain Project Diversion matters had been handled directly by then IDAC head Advocate Andrea Johnson and described being informed of matters after the fact. He also took the commission through IDAC's case selection criteria manual, which is intended to guard against political interference, and said it was an approved document rather than a draft, but that it lacked adequate consequences for procedural failures. Justice Madlanga noted this was the second occasion on which Sesoko had been stripped of authority.

summary: The Commission sat at the Brigitte Mabandla Justice College and opened by granting, on agreement between the parties, a postponement of Mr Tumelo Nku's scheduled testimony to 18 June 2026 following a family bereavement. Chief Inspector Samuel Mashaba continued his testimony, first clarifying details of a 2021 Aeroton incident involving an alleged drug-carrying truck and his calls to senior SAPS officers, then facing extended questioning from the Chairperson and Commissioners on the legal limits of a traffic officer's law-enforcement powers. Evidence leaders then put an extensive WhatsApp record between Mashaba and businessman Mr Nku, dating from 2019, to him, including exhibits (CJC274.3, CJC275.1) purporting to show Mashaba directing named SAPS members to perform paid, unofficial recovery and investigative work for Nku -- including in relation to cash and property reported stolen at an airport -- and a message in which Mashaba told Nku they should keep working so he could 'look after' the newly appointed Gauteng MEC for Community Safety, Faith Mazibuko. Mashaba confirmed the phone number and many of the messages as his own but repeatedly said he could not recall the underlying events, prompting sharp exchanges with the Chairperson and Commissioners about the plausibility of his memory lapses.

witnesses.role_as_described: Assistant Director, IPID National Specialized Investigative Team; investigated the defeating-the-ends-of-justice complaint (Booysens CAS 252/10/2021) laid by Chief Mashaba, Warrant Officer Magane and Warrant Officer Phakula

summary: The Commission resumed testimony from Lt-Col Sebola, who read a supplementary affidavit and was taken through an analyst-prepared presentation of cellphone/Threema/WhatsApp/Telegram screenshots said to link Tumelo Nku, an individual saved as 'Alpha', and Samuel Mashaba (saved in Nku's phone as 'General Mashaba of Hawks') to surveillance and movement of shipping containers, including an apparent earlier attempt in May 2021 and the Aeroton consignment in July 2021. Commissioners repeatedly found Sebola unable to explain key features of the presentation (including how Threema screenshots were distinguished from WhatsApp ones, and the meaning of call-diagrams linking Mashaba, Phokungwana and Magane) and asked that a comprehensive statement be obtained from the analyst who compiled it. Sebola also gave evidence on IPID's and General Gerber's and Major-General Kadwa's respective findings on the DPCI's conduct, on DPCI's refusal to hand IPID the docket, and alleged senior-official interference in the Booysens investigation, while conceding several administrative/evidentiary errors flagged by General Gerber. In the afternoon, IPID Assistant Director Takalani Maphosho was sworn in and read her statement on IPID's investigation into the complaint of defeating the ends of justice at the Aeroton scene, describing the arrests of Magane, Phakula and Mashaba by DPCI members led by General Khan and General Kadwa, the release of the truck driver, receiving clerk (Jolene Koekemoer) and warehouse manager, and DPCI's persistent refusal (escalated to Generals Sekgobela, Kadwa and Lebeya) to provide IPID with the Booysens docket. Commissioners pressed Maphosho hard on IPID's failure to verify Nku's claimed status as an 'informer', its lack of scrutiny of the complainants' own conduct and jurisdiction, and the basis for concluding the arresting DPCI officers (rather than the original three) had defeated the ends of justice, given that no one, on the Commissioners' analysis, should have been arrested that day.

witnesses.role_as_described: Lieutenant Colonel (now Colonel) in the DPCI, at the time of the June 2021 seizure the Investigating Officer on a 541kg Cocaine seizure at the CHC Container Depot, Durban; now Unit Commander of Durban's COCIU (comprising the National Priority Violent Crime Section, SANEB and EPR). Continuing testimony begun the previous sitting day.

summary: Colonel Jacob continued his cross-examination on the 2021 CHC Depot Cocaine seizure and the subsequent theft of the exhibits from a Port Shepstone office. Evidence leader Adv Sello SC and Commissioners Baloyi and Khumalo used a DPCI presentation and Captain Moolman's statement to show that Maydon Wharf accommodated 999kg of Cocaine six weeks after Jacob's seizure, undermining his claim to have 'exhausted all avenues' for storage in Durban before the exhibits were moved to Port Shepstone; Jacob ultimately conceded the assumption was wrong and not based on fact, and that telling his Brigadier he had exhausted all avenues was, factually, untrue. He also conceded there was no justification for not calling the LCRC (forensic) unit to the scene, and that the reliability of the investigation diary compiled by Warrant Officer Mpangase was open to serious doubt on several points, including an unrecorded decision to detain the container and the sequencing of when the 27kg/kilogram drug quantity became known. At the start of the day the Commission granted, by agreement between the parties, a partially in-camera arrangement for a protected witness ('Witness I') to testify by audio link with visual features concealed on 9 June, over a media objection from Daily Maverick and News24. Housekeeping at the end of the day recorded that Major General Senona's evidence, scheduled for the next sitting, was postponed to a date in the week of 8 June 2026 due to counsel's illness.

rulings.description: By agreement between the parties, Witness I's application for his evidence to be heard partially in camera on 9 June 2026 was granted: his testimony will be heard publicly via audio link with his face/visual features concealed, and media and other persons present are prohibited from publishing any image or footage that may reveal or tend to reveal his identity.

Commissioners pressed him on contradictions between his statement and earlier evidence about Isipingo's storage capacity, on the absence of any diary entry recording his account of a key phone call, and on the fact that no full quantitative or qualitative FSL analysis of the substance was ever completed before it was stolen. The sitting was adjourned to resume the next morning, with his testimony still incomplete.

summary: Warrant Officer Marumo Magane, an office-bound SAPS crime-statistics officer, testified about how he was drawn into a July 2021 drug interdiction after Gauteng Traffic Chief Samuel Mashaba asked him for manpower, and how the two men, together with an informant (Mr Tumelo Nku), followed a container truck without a warrant from Roodekop to a Scania warehouse in Aeroton before opening it and finding roughly 23 bags of suspected cocaine. Commissioners Baloyi and Khumalo took Magane in detail through repeated departures from the National Instruction on Crime Scene Management -- no cordon, no photographs before opening, no gloves, exhibits moved and handled by multiple untrained people before LCRC was called -- which Magane repeatedly conceded amounted to a 'stuff-up'. He described how Major General Feroz Khan of Crime Intelligence then arrived, disarmed Mashaba, and had Magane, Mashaba, Phakula and Nku arrested and detained for about two weeks, leading to departmental charges (later dismissed) and a criminal case that was provisionally withdrawn in 2022 but which a 2024/2025 NPA letter suggests may be reinstated. Commissioner Baloyi closed by putting to Magane a series of propositions -- including unexplained WhatsApp messages referencing a spare seal and R60,000 cash found in the informant's BMW -- suggesting he may, wittingly or not, have been used to help intercept the drugs rather than have them properly processed; Magane maintained his innocence throughout.

witnesses.name: Colonel Francois Steyn
witnesses.role_as_described: Unit Commander, West Rand Serious Organised Crime Unit, SAPS/DPCI; Provincial Coordinator for SANEB (South African Narcotics Enforcement Bureau) and Kidnapping for Ransom investigations, Gauteng

summary: Colonel Francois Steyn testified about narcotics enforcement challenges generally before giving detailed evidence on the 9 July 2021 Aeroton drug bust, in which roughly 700-715 kilograms of cocaine were found in a Scania container shipped via Durban from Santos, Brazil, using a 'rip-on-rip-off' smuggling method requiring corrupt law enforcement involvement. He described a chaotic, poorly cordoned crime scene involving a Traffic Chief, two police officers and a civilian informant who allegedly tried to remove the drugs before Booysens SAPS intervened, and detailed discrepancies in the exhibit count (684/700/715 bricks) across the SAP13 register, forensic intake and later a discovery that 136.46 kilograms (roughly R55 million) of the cocaine was unaccounted for by February 2025 while in FSL custody. He also discussed the IPID recommendation for disciplinary proceedings against himself and four other DPCI/SAPS officials, Major General Gerber's departmental investigation which exonerated them but flagged administrative errors, and a February 2025 media leak of internal WhatsApp evidence linking the informant to a Durban-port businessman.

He then read his supplementary statement comparing the seizure to other 2020-2022 Durban drug busts, concluding the Port Shepstone cocaine should never have been stored there, and stated General Senona ought to have been polygraph-tested given his active role. summary: The Commission opened with an application by Adv Sello SC, on behalf of the Evidence Leaders, for the Friday witness on the Port Shepstone drug theft (a matter involving 541kg of cocaine) to testify fully in camera, out of concern that public testimony would jeopardise ongoing investigations, confidential sources and potential future prosecutions. The Chairperson granted condonation for short notice and issued a rule nisi, ordering the application be served on media by 14:00 that day with a response deadline of 14:00 on 7 May 2026, to be finalised on 8 May 2026 if opposed. The Commission then began a new evidentiary stream on drug seizures, hearing sworn testimony from Maj-Gen Hendrik Flynn, DPCI Component Head for Serious Organised Crime, who gave background on DPCI structure, illicit drug trafficking methods (including the 'rip-on-rip-off' technique), and then detailed the 22 June 2021 seizure of 541kg of cocaine in Durban and its theft from the DPCI Port Shepstone strongroom between 6-8 November 2021. Flynn testified, under extensive Commissioner questioning about a sequence of security failures (improper crime scene handling, storage at Port Shepstone despite closer facilities and precedent for storing larger seizures at Isipingo, an unrenewed security contract, a non-functioning alarm, and key-control irregularities involving Maj-Gen Senona), that he believed the theft was 'by design' and not mere coincidence.

summary: The day opened with housekeeping: Inspector Phiri was recalled and excused to appear instead on 20 April 2026 pending a signed statement, and witness Gareth Mnisi's appearance was interposed to 17 April 2026 by agreement between evidence leaders and his counsel. The bulk of the day was the sworn testimony of TMPD Director Tshukudu Malatji, who was led through his statement on the 2016-2017 TMPD2 security-services tender (won after a 2021 Court Order by 22 providers including Triotic and Gubis 85), the circumstances in which bid documents were moved from Supply Chain Management premises to a college venue, and his role as a Bid Evaluation Committee member and tender contact person. Commissioners repeatedly pressed Malatji on why, despite becoming aware in December 2024 of irregular ad hoc security deployments to Gubis 85 (allocated by Inspector Phiri without proper authority), he did not act on a 12 March 2025 written instruction from Deputy Chief Revo Spies to halt all ad hoc deployments, a delay that cost the City of Tshwane roughly R14-17 million a month until termination letters were finally issued in June 2025. Malatji also made unproven "suspicions" of an irregular recruitment process behind Spies's appointment, which commissioners pressed him to substantiate or drop, and asked the Commission's help accessing TMPD records for a supplementary statement given restrictions from his ongoing suspension.

rulings.description: Inspector A.L. Phiri, recalled but not yet ready to testify, was excused for the day and directed to appear instead on 20 April 2026, with a signed and finalised statement to be submitted at least five days beforehand.

Witness Gareth Mnisi, present under subpoena, was excused with his appearance interposed to 17 April 2026 at 09:30, after evidence leaders and his counsel (Adv Van Den Heever) agreed on the new date and bundle-exchange timeline.

Director Malatji was ruled to be at liberty to supplement his statement with further documents once the evidence leaders assist him to access them, with the Commission to decide later whether that takes the form of a supplemented statement or further oral testimony.

witnesses.name: Revo Spies
witnesses.role_as_described: Deputy Chief of Police for Asset Protection and Security Services, Tshwane Metropolitan Police Department (TMPD); previously testified before the Commission in the Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Police Department stream

summary: Commissioner (Deputy Chief) Revo Spies of the Tshwane Metropolitan Police Department testified about the TMPD 2/2016/17 physical security guarding tender, its irregular procurement history, litigation, and repeated month-to-month extensions that kept the same 22 companies in place for years past the original three-year term. He detailed how ad hoc security services, ostensibly emergency deployments, were used to funnel a disproportionate share of work and payment (around R59 million over one year, plus purchase orders totalling roughly R13.6 million created in a suspicious cluster on 6 March 2025) to one company, Gubis85 Solutions, and described email exchanges implicating CFO Gareth Mnisi and Deputy Commissioner Umashi Dhlamini in the escalation. Spies also testified about a Metro Police inspector, Lebogang/AL Phiri, issuing deployment letters he had no authority to issue, his own instructions to halt the ad hoc deployments, the suspension of Director Tshukudu Malatji, and referrals of the matter to internal affairs, Group Audit and Risk, and the Hawks. He briefly covered a second, land-invasion-related tender (TMPD 1/2024-25) involving Ngaphesheya Construction and Projects, and closed with remarks about victimisation of whistleblowers within TMPD.

summary: Sergeant Nkosi continued his cross-examination, focused mainly on an FNB bank card linked to Mr Cat Matlala that Nkosi said he found in a jet ski, where evidence leaders and Commissioners confronted him with multiple contradictory versions (on timing, who alerted whom, and where it was found) and with ATM withdrawals in December 2024 suggesting he had personal use of the card. He was also questioned about R385,000 in cash found in his safe during an October 2024 raid, which he attributed to a truck sale by his brother, but the supporting documents (sale agreement, affidavits) contained date and detail inconsistencies suggesting they were prepared after the fact. Further questioning covered a R500 payment to a journalist referred to as "Natasha SABC" for a phone number, video footage of him collecting a bag from Mr Katiso Molefe's house that he initially said (in his statement) he returned to Harley-Davidson but later admitted he never did, and his role relaying messages between Mr Matlala and General Sibiya, including regarding impalas allegedly delivered to Sibiya's farm. The Chair excused the witness at the end of the day pending a decision on whether re-examination would proceed.

summary: On Day 79 (17 March 2026), cross-examination of Sergeant Fannie Nkosi by Adv Chaskalson SC continued, working through his WhatsApp exchanges with General Sibiya, businessman Steve Motsumi, General Shibiri and General Mkhwanazi. Nkosi was pressed on why he repeatedly forwarded news articles and internal SAPS material about General Khumalo, General Masemola and General Mkhwanazi to Motsumi, a civilian, and on an internal SAPS report naming a complainant, a witness and arrested suspects in a Mooinooi chrome-theft case that he shared with Motsumi two days before the suspects' first court appearance; the Chairperson and Commissioners Khumalo and Baloyi repeatedly found his explanations unsatisfactory or evasive. Extensive questioning also covered Nkosi's proximity to Mr Matlala around the 6 December 2024 raid on Matlala's house (including a suspected tip-off, which Nkosi denied while confirming he was on the phone with Matlala when the Special Task Force arrived), a media enquiry about kidnapping figure Esmael Nangy that Sibiya asked Nkosi to route to Matlala, an alleged 2022 attempt by Matlala on the life of Mr Sibanyoni, and a photograph of an internal SAPS personnel screen -- showing the home address of the officer investigating Matlala and Mr Molefe -- that Nkosi said an informant introduced by General Shibiri had given him, an account Chaskalson confronted with chat metadata suggesting the chronology and authorship were false. The day opened and later paused twice on disputes, resolved by Chairperson's rulings, over documents and chat material referred to by the evidence leaders that had not been placed in Mr Ngoato's paginated bundle.

rulings.description: On the morning dispute over attorneys having approached Sergeant Nkosi and amended his file bundle overnight without notice to his attorney, Mr Ngoato: the Chairperson recorded Adv Chaskalson's concession that this was wrong and his undertaking it would not recur, and confirmed that none of the newly added bank statements or handwritten statements would be used that day.

Ruled that it was fair for the evidence leaders to put Sergeant Nkosi's WhatsApp chats with General Mkhwanazi to him, even though those chats were on a disclosed memory stick rather than in the paginated bundle, because the witness's own evidence had made them relevant; directed Adv Chaskalson to provide the relevant extract (about 35 pages) to Mr Ngoato by tea time.

On Mr Ngoato's renewed objection that chats with an unnamed Pakistani informant (used to challenge Nkosi's account of a SAPS personnel-screen photograph) were not in his bundle, ruled that cross-examination should continue without a stop-start pause since the line arose from the witness's own answers, while directing that the underlying chat material be made available to Mr Ngoato to consult and potentially use in re-examination.

witnesses.role_as_described: SAPS sergeant, formerly attached to the Deputy National Commissioner for Crime Detection's office; previously anonymised in Commission proceedings as 'Witness F'; continuing cross-examination on his relationship with Mr Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala, Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya, Brigadier Ramangwa, General Fannie, Brigadier Glenda Bokaba, General Shibiri, Mr Zenzile 'Ze' Nxumalo and Mr Motsumi

summary: The day opened with the Chairperson reading reasons for his 13 March 2026 order recalling the earlier ruling that had allowed Sergeant Nkosi to testify remotely, off-camera and without his name being used; the Chair held that continued anonymity was no longer justified because Nkosi's identity and image had already entered the public domain via a video clip played during General Khumalo's testimony and inadvertent references by Nkosi's own attorney and an evidence leader, and Nkosi then testified for the first time in open session under his own name. Adv Chaskalson SC resumed cross-examination on outstanding topics from Nkosi's February testimony, including the timing of Mr Matlala's first meeting with Lt-Gen Sibiya, Nkosi's forwarding of a warrant of arrest and other suspect information for Mr Musa Khawula to complainant Mr Zenzile Nxumalo, and an unsuccessful undercover operation in which six SAPS members travelled to a Kroonstad concert on tickets bought by Nxumalo to try to arrest Khawula. Extensive questioning also covered Nkosi's practice of forwarding internal and confidential SAPS communications -- including a confidential audit report recommending termination of Mr Matlala's SAPS contract -- to Mr Matlala, General Shibiri and Mr Matlala's associate/creditor Mr Motsumi, and Nkosi's frequent, code-gated visits to Mr Motsumi's Waterfall Estate home, often with fellow officers who were then sent vehicle registration numbers to trace. The Commissioners repeatedly put to Nkosi that his conduct suggested Nxumalo and Matlala were effectively directing police action and that state resources had been misused for private benefit, which Nkosi largely denied while attributing contradictions to memory lapses on his and General Sibiya's part; the hearing adjourned to resume on 17 March 2026.

rulings.description: Recalling the order of 30 January 2026 (as repeated on 3 February 2026), the Chairperson directed that Sergeant Nkosi appear physically and testify in open session under his own name, holding that his identity and image were already public and that his witness statement and evidence did not implicate anyone in a way that would justify continued remote, off-camera, anonymised testimony; reasons for the underlying 13 March 2026 order were read into the record at the start of the day.

summary: Day 77 (13 March 2026, a Friday, held at Brigitte Mabandla Justice College) continued the cross-examination of SAPS Lt-Gen Shibiri on a recorded December 2024 phone call with an investigating officer, 'Witness A', concerning the murder of Armand Swart and the arrest of Katiso Molefe. Evidence leaders pressed Shibiri on shifting explanations for who Deputy National Commissioner Lt-Gen Sibiya wanted information for ('the other side'), on his now-confirmed reference to a 'group of five' business associates of the late Mr Mswazi (including Molefe), on figures named 'Joe' and 'Zee', and on whether a district-level official he described as interfering in the investigation was Brigadier Nkhwashu. The Commission also examined a R53,538 suit purchase Shibiri denied was a gift from implicated businessmen, and heard his stated reluctance, on safety grounds, to name certain individuals publicly. Separately, counsel for a prospective witness, 'Witness G', applied for partially in-camera, off-camera testimony to protect that witness's identity; the Commission made no ruling, directing counsel to prepare a joint protocol with public notice, and stood the matter down until 16 March 2026.

rulings.description: No order made on the application for 'Witness G' to testify partially in camera and off-camera; the Commission directed evidence leader Adv Chaskalson SC and Witness G's counsel, Mr Matlala, to jointly draft a protocol to be publicised with at least 72 hours' notice to the media before any restriction takes effect, with the matter stood down until 16 March 2026.

Placed on record that the Commission is not responsible for the composition of the task team appointed to investigate SAPS members implicated in the Commission's proceedings; the Commission's role was limited to making referrals.

summary: On Day 76 (12 March 2026, held at the Brigitte Mabandla Justice College), cross-examination of Lt-Gen Richard Shibiri continued, centred on his account of a personal loan from businessman Vusi Matlala used to pay for accident repairs. The Chairperson and evidence leaders used Shibiri's own bank and credit-card statements to argue that he and his son already had well over R100,000 available at the time, undermining his stated need for the loan, and put WhatsApp messages to him suggesting he had expected Matlala to attend the September 2024 gathering at which the loan arose. Proceedings were adjourned in the late afternoon, before cross-examination was complete, to resume at 9:30 the next morning, 13 March 2026.

summary: Sitting at the Brigitte Mabandla Justice College, the Commission heard the sworn testimony of businessman Suleiman Carrim, who advanced R10 million to Vusi Matlala's Medicare 24 Tshwane District SAPS contract and admitted fabricating a close relationship with Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, on the advice of Oupa 'Brown' Mogotsi, to pressure Matlala into repaying him. Evidence leader Adv Chaskalson SC used WhatsApp and banking records to challenge Carrim's claim that Matlala had been 'avoiding' him and to probe R500,000-R750,000 in payments routed via Tameez Investments to Luthaga Trading Enterprise for the benefit of Morgan Maumela, raising a possible money-laundering issue under section 5 of POCA over Adv Bhana SC's objection that this exceeded the Commission's mandate; the Chairperson allowed the questioning to continue at this stage. Before the afternoon session the Commission also granted an unopposed application postponing further testimony by Brigadier Mkhwanazi to 23 March 2026, citing preparation time and a scheduled eye operation. The day opened with the Chairperson recording an earlier off-camera altercation and mutual apologies among counsel and refusing interlocutory relief sought on Matlala's behalf regarding late document production; Carrim's cross-examination is set to continue on the next sitting day.

summary: Day 72 (6 March 2026) was devoted entirely to legal argument on an interlocutory application brought by Suleiman Carrim, through counsel Adv Premhid, seeking that his forthcoming evidence (scheduled for 9-10 March) be heard in camera on the grounds of threats received against him, his family and his businesses. After the Chairperson refused, in open session, a preliminary request that the in-camera application itself be argued in camera, the Commission heard full argument on the merits from Adv Premhid and from evidence leader Adv Hassim SC, with extensive questioning from the Chairperson and Commissioners Baloyi SC and Khumalo SC probing the factual basis for the threats, their connection (or lack of one) to the Commission, and whether in-camera relief would actually protect Carrim given his identity and testimony dates are already public. The Commission reserved a combined written ruling on both the morning's preliminary point and the afternoon's merits argument for 9:30am Monday 9 March 2026, and directed that any supplementary affidavit from Carrim addressing the possible source of the threats be filed by midday Saturday 7 March, with any evidence-leader response due by 7pm that day.

summary: The Commission opened by declining to hear Mr Mogotsi, whose vague medical certificate drew sharp criticism from the Chairperson, who said the Commission may refer such certificates to the medical regulatory council and question doctors in a private session; Mogotsi's testimony was postponed. The Commission then heard the sworn evidence of Maj-Gen Richard Shibiri, suspended Component Head of SAPS Organised Crime Investigation, who read through his statement responding to a Commission summons covering alleged criminal-syndicate infiltration of law enforcement, his relationship with businessman Vusi 'Cat' Matlala (including a loan he says he repaid) and self-described traditional healer Vusi Makhubela, a 16 May 2024 briefing to detectives investigating the Vereeniging/Armand Swart murder case (the disputed 'envelope strategy' allegation), contact relating to journalist Musa Khawula, the SAPS-Medicare24 Tshwane contract, and allegations he improperly disclosed bail information about Warrant Officer Michael Pule Tau. Shibiri denied orchestrating or suggesting bribery and denied influencing bail decisions, while confirming some elements of disputed conversations and alleging that a colleague, Sergeant Daniel Motaung, was improperly induced with a promised promotion to give adverse information against him. The hearing, punctuated by several adjournments and on-record corrections to Shibiri's written statement, stood down for Thursday and is set to resume his testimony on Friday, 6 March 2026.

rulings.description: Mr Mogotsi's testimony was postponed to a date to be determined, after the Chairperson found his medical certificate inadequate; the Commission indicated it is considering referring the certificate to the medical regulatory council and questioning the doctor in a private session.

exhibits.description: Sergeant Ndlela's sworn affidavit (deposed 7 July 2025), which Shibiri says confirms the true nature of his 16 May 2024 briefing to detectives; Commissioner Khumalo SC disputed that the affidavit actually disputes any suggestion of bribery.

Bank statement and mechanic's proof-of-deposit/quotation documents Shibiri says support his account of the loan from Matlala and its use for his son's vehicle repairs.

summary: The Commission convened on 2 March 2026 expecting testimony from Mr Mogotsi on topics not yet canvassed before the Commission or Parliament, but that morning he informed the Commission he was ill and undertook to provide a medical certificate later in the day. The Chairperson stated that, absent the certificate, Mogotsi was in contempt and the panel had intended to initiate legal process against him immediately, but at Adv Chaskalson's request the Commission held off and stood the matter down. Mogotsi, previously legally represented before the Commission, is no longer represented. The Commission adjourned early after noting it would not sit on 3 March 2026 due to a panel member's unavailability, and would resume on Wednesday 4 March 2026 with General Shibiri testifying, at which time Mogotsi's non-appearance would also be considered.

witnesses.role_as_described: Head of Department: Human Resources, City of Ekurhuleni (currently suspended); testimony continuing from the previous sitting day

summary: Ekurhuleni HR head Linda Gxasheka continued her testimony, extensively cross-examined on the City's award of a R66,500 training tender to Buena Vista Learning Academy (formerly a shisanyama called Mokoko Grill, sole director Tsakani Baloyi, partner of Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala) which ultimately received almost R3.5 million; she conceded numerous features of the bid — a director appointed days before the advertisement, a name change weeks before closing, accreditation and reference letters belonging to other companies, VAT and turnover discrepancies — were red flags that should have led to disqualification, while denying personal involvement in the adjudicating committees. She was also pressed at length on the repeatedly stalled 2023 disciplinary charges against Brigadier (later Deputy Chief) Julius Mkhwanazi — including a charge that he allowed Cat Matlala's company CAT Security to use unlawfully obtained blue-light vehicles — on his subsequent promotion and roughly R200,000 salary increase despite the charges never being resolved, and on an arbitration award (in Deputy Chief Revo Spies's favour) that found the City had acted in bad faith in suspending him, prompting Gxasheka to withdraw an earlier 'fraud' allegation against Spies. A same-day, unsworn statement from former HR project manager Makosi Makamba, disputing Gxasheka's account of the tender process, was admitted over defence objection for questioning, with the chairperson directing that the underlying letter it referenced be sourced.

rulings.description: Declined the witness's request, made at the start of the day, to postpone/roll the hearing over to 2 March because of newly received documents (a tender bundle, transcript extracts, a two-page letter, and a 14-page arbitration award); after establishing the tender bundle had been available since the Wednesday, directed the parties to use a short adjournment to paginate and identify relevant pages and to begin evidence that morning.

Over objection from the witness's counsel (Ms Magula) that a same-day, unsworn four-page statement from Makosi Makamba was not a proper affidavit and referenced an unattached letter, ruled the evidence leader could put its contents to the witness for comment, while directing that all endeavours be made to source the letter/annexures it referred to.

Directed that the full psychometric/competency assessment record for Brigadier Mkhwanazi, which the witness had cited but only shown in part, be provided to the Commission as part of the record, with handling of its sensitivity to be discussed with the evidence leaders.

summary: The day opened with a renewed postponement application for an unnamed witness, after the Chairperson queried discrepancies between two medical certificates; the Commission postponed that witness's appearance to 11 March 2026 and ordered a statement by 3 March 2026. The Commission then affirmed Linda Gxasheka, Ekurhuleni's HOD Human Resources, who was led by the evidence leader through her supplementary sworn statement responding to a Rule 3 Notice alleging she supported the usurpation of the Chief of Police's statutory powers and interfered with the disciplinary process against then-Brigadier (later Deputy Chief of Police) Julius Mkhwanazi, including a suspension tied to vehicles allegedly linked to "CAT VIP" registered to the municipal fleet. Gxasheka denied usurping powers, described the interview panel that appointed Ms Stella Jokazi, the 2023 suspension and later upliftment of Mkhwanazi's suspension, disputed email evidence about service of his charge sheet, an internal forensic report and legal opinion on the matter, and testified about fearing for her safety. The sitting was adjourned before cross-examination ("intrusive questioning") began, to allow her legal team time to review documents disclosed late, and the hearing was set to resume at 9:30 the next morning.

rulings.description: The unnamed witness's appearance was postponed to 11 March 2026, with a new subpoena to be served, and the witness's statement was ordered to be furnished to the Commission by 3 March 2026.

summary: Day 67 of the Madlanga Commission, held at the Brigitte Mabandla Justice College, did not proceed with oral evidence: the scheduled witness, a Crime Intelligence officer who handles agents and informants and whose name was withheld at this stage, had fallen ill, and his legal representatives brought a postponement application. Evidence leader Adv Chaskalson SC and the Chairperson both found the supporting medical certificate largely illegible and lacking detail on the nature of the illness, and Commissioner Adv Baloyi SC warned against a recurring pattern of inadequate certificates being used to postpone witnesses. The Chairperson stood the application down for a day, directing that a clearer certificate and a confirmatory affidavit from the witness be produced, and the sitting adjourned to 26 February 2026 at 9:30 rather than proceeding with the next scheduled witness.

Matter was adjourned to 26 February 2026 at 9:30, without the Commission substituting the next scheduled witness in the interim, so as not to disrupt the schedule of another witness who had already been rescheduled.

witnesses.role_as_described: Suspended Deputy National Commissioner of Police (Head: Detective Services) and former Acting National Commissioner; continuing cross-examination on his relationship with Sergeant Nkosi, General Shibiri, Vusimuzi Matlala and businessman Steve Motsumi, and on a confidential SAPS audit report into Matlala's contract

summary: Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya continued a full day of cross-examination before the Madlanga Commission, focused on WhatsApp evidence showing Sergeant Nkosi acting as an intermediary between Sibiya, General Shibiri, businessman Steve Motsumi and implicated person Vusimuzi Matlala. Evidence leader Hassim and Commissioners Baloyi and Khumalo questioned Sibiya about a private September 2024 engagement party at his home attended by Matlala, Shibiri and Nkosi, about his forwarding of a confidential SAPS audit report recommending termination of Matlala's health-services contract (which was then relayed on to Matlala, Shibiri and Motsumi), and about payments and meetings arranged through Nkosi with taxi-industry figures. Sibiya repeatedly complained the process was one-sided given the seizure of his devices, prompting the Chair to confirm his lawyers were not legally barred from accessing the subpoenaed devices. The sitting adjourned, with Sibiya citing mental exhaustion, just as evidence leader Hassim was about to begin questioning him on allegations of a 'potentially corrupt relationship' with Brown Mogotsi; his testimony was postponed to a later date.

rulings.description: Chair confirmed there was no legal bar to Lt-Gen Sibiya's legal representatives accessing his subpoenaed electronic devices (then held by an independent third party assessing a search-and-seizure challenge) to assist his ongoing testimony, and urged that access be pursued before his testimony resumes

summary: Lt-Gen Sibiya continued his testimony, with the Chair first refusing his request to postpone his cross-examination until Witness F recovered and completed his own testimony, citing the Commission's 17 March deadline. Evidence leader Adv Hassim SC then led Sibiya through WhatsApp records showing Sergeant Fannie Nkosi (Witness F) acting as an intermediary between Sibiya and Mr Matlala ('Cat'), including a March 2024 exchange in which a farm manager appears to have been paid by Matlala to deliver impala antelope to Sibiya's residence; Sibiya denied ever receiving impalas from Matlala despite photographs he had sent to General Senthumule showing two impalas dying on his property on 27 March 2024, days after the arranged delivery date. Sibiya was also questioned about Matlala and his wife attending his son's September 2024 engagement party at his invitation, and about Sergeant Nkosi forwarding a warrant of arrest for social-media commentator Musa Khawula to Matlala's security company, which Sibiya denied instructing but agreed would be improper. The day closed with Sibiya conceding that part of his written statement describing no working relationship with Sergeant Nkosi was inaccurate.

rulings.description: Refused Lt-Gen Sibiya's request to postpone his cross-examination until Witness F's testimony (interrupted by illness) was completed; ruled that questioning would continue as structured by the evidence leader given the Commission's scheduling pressure to conclude by 17 March 2026.

witnesses.role_as_described: Deputy National Commissioner: Crime Detection, South African Police Service; continuing cross-examination begun on Day 63 concerning the disbandment of the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) and the transfer/handling of its case dockets

summary: Cross-examination of Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya continued from the previous day, centred on the disbandment of the KZN/Eastern Cape Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) and the transfer of its 121 case dockets. Evidence leader Adv Hassim SC and Commissioners Baloyi SC and Khumalo SC pressed Sibiya on whether his letters of 17 January, 4 February and 22 April 2025 directing that all PKTT dockets (including those on the court roll) be transferred to Lt-Gen Senthumule were authorised by National Commissioner Masemola or by the Minister-approved disbandment/action plan, or reflected his own initiative; Sibiya eventually conceded his instruction on court-going dockets was at odds with the approved plan and that the 3 January 2025 Letogo email (SS9/SS10) he had repeatedly relied on did not, on its face, instruct him to "implement" deactivation. The Commission also tested Sibiya's reliance on an unsigned audit report (SS23) to claim PKTT dockets had been neglected, with Commissioner Khumalo pointing to errors in that document when compared against the signed 28 March 2025 handover report, and Sibiya ultimately agreeing (from a stated neutral standpoint) that the dockets sitting un-investigated at head office for months amounted to serious interference with the administration of justice. The sitting was adjourned mid-afternoon before a new topic could begin, to resume the following Monday, 23 February 2026.

rulings.description: A newly received further statement relevant to Sibiya's evidence (File 10C, marked exhibit CJC81) was noted as handed in; the Chairperson directed that it be set aside for the witness's legal team to review during the lunch adjournment before being put to the witness.

exhibits.description: A further statement relevant to Lt-Gen Sibiya's evidence, handed in as an exhibit at the start of the day; it had already been shared with the witness's legal team shortly before the sitting.

witnesses.name: Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya
witnesses.role_as_described: Deputy National Commissioner: Crime Detection, SAPS (currently suspended); implicated in the PKTT disbandment, the Matlala search-and-seizure matters, and related allegations

summary: Lieutenant-General Shadrack Sibiya, continuing testimony begun on a previous day, read the remainder of his affidavit into the record, responding to the evidence of General Khumalo, Witness C (Matlala), Witness F, and General Senthumule, and raising further allegations concerning the National Commissioner, General Senthumule, and General Mosikili. He was then cross-examined at length on the disbandment of the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT), including the Marais Report/work-study document (Exhibit SS47) and the minutes of a 1 November 2024 meeting with then-Minister Mchunu, and was repeatedly unable to point to any passage recommending the PKTT's disbandment, conceding that no formal review of the PKTT or consultation with General Khumalo preceded the 31 December 2024 decision. Evidence leader Adv Hassim SC and Commissioners Baloyi and Khumalo pressed Sibiya on his own 17 January 2025 letter to Khumalo, which ordered an immediate change in reporting lines and demanded a close-out report on a timeline that predated the letter's own signature date. An audio recording of a phone call between Sibiya and General Senthumule was played into the record, and Sibiya also addressed a white BMW allegedly linked to Matlala's residence, devices seized from him, and pending challenges to two search-and-seizure warrants.

rulings.description: The Chair directed that a witness discussed in Sibiya's affidavit not be named, ruling that he be referred to only as 'Witness F' to avoid effectively identifying a protected witness through association.

The Chair directed that Sibiya should not ventilate several additional, un-pleaded allegations against other witnesses ad hoc while reading his statement, and should instead confer with his legal team, with a possible brief supplementary affidavit as the appropriate vehicle.

summary: Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya, sworn in as the day's witness, continued his evidence-in-chief, reading through his statement covering his career history, prior dismissal and reinstatement, the high treason/espionage and fraudulent-claims allegations against him, the City of Johannesburg spying-equipment controversy, and his suspension over the disbandment of the Political Killing Task Team (PKTT). He maintained that National Commissioner Masemola knew of and directed the PKTT's disbandment and that Sibiya's own role was confined to implementing instructions relayed through Brigadier Letogo and Maj-Gen Rabie. witnesses.role_as_described: IPID (Independent Police Investigative Directorate) investigator attached to the Ekurhuleni team, investigating misconduct by members of the Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Police Department (EMPD) -- continuing and concluding multi-day testimony begun on a prior sitting day, taking the Commission through a series of EMPD case dockets and responding to allegations by Chief Isaac Mapiyeye and Commissioner Revo Spies that IPID stalled or protected EMPD members, including suspended EMPD acting chief Brigadier Julius Mkhwanazi

summary: IPID investigator Thulani Magagula continued and concluded his testimony, taking the Commission through a run of EMPD (Ekurhuleni Metro Police) misconduct dockets -- a truck and cargo theft in Putfontein (CAS86/02/2023), a cigarette-theft kidnapping in Benoni (CAS215-07-2022), a seized semi-precious-stones matter in Hillbrow (CAS797-03-2023), and an extortion case against a Congolese businessman in Boksburg North (CAS241-03-2024, now on trial) -- and explained IPID's practice of holding disciplinary recommendations to EMPD until a criminal investigation is finalised, which the Chairperson repeatedly suggested was an unduly cautious misreading of IPID's own procedure and which Magagula accepted he may have gotten wrong. Much of the day addressed Chief Mapiyeye and Commissioner Spies's allegations, raised in a 26 January 2024 letter, that Magagula had an improper relationship with Brigadier Julius Mkhwanazi and that IPID was deliberately stalling probes -- including the earlier 'blue lights' case tied to Vusimuzi Matlala and the Brakpan murder of Emmanuel Mbense -- which Magagula denied, describing the Mkhwanazi contact as official (a training session on IPID firearm-seizure procedure) and citing a backlog of 727 cases across a six-investigator team. His testimony concluded the day and the Commission adjourned to 16 February 2026.

reporting_context.claim: EWN reported that IPID assistant director Thulani Magagula used his 13 February 2026 testimony to directly refute claims that IPID undermined or delayed investigations into EMPD officials, specifically addressing the Brakpan murder of Emmanuel Mbense and the blue-lights-on-vehicles matter linked to Vusimuzi Matlala, and confirmed meeting Revo Spies, suspended EMPD head Isaac Mapiyeye and Colonel Hennie Erasmus to discuss the blue lights case.

IOL reported that Magagula rejected allegations by retired Ekurhuleni deputy commissioner Revo Spies that IPID deliberately undermined probes into senior EMPD officials, and specifically denied stalling or weakening investigations that could have implicated suspended EMPD acting chief Julius Mkhwanazi, telling the Commission he would demonstrate the allegations were factually incorrect.

IOL reported that Magagula told the Commission an EMPD officer (Cummings) convicted of repeatedly raping young girls remained on active duty throughout his criminal trial and was dismissed only after conviction and multiple life sentences, which Magagula framed as reflecting a wider departmental pattern of EMPD waiting for criminal outcomes rather than acting on IPID's evidence.

SABC News covered a dispute between IPID and the City of Ekurhuleni over an EMPD theft case, consistent with the day's testimony on the Putfontein truck/cargo theft investigation; the outlet's full article text could not be retrieved to confirm further detail.

summary: Continuing his cross-examination, Advocate Kemi Behari, Head of Risk and Legal at the City of Ekurhuleni, was confronted with a newly disclosed email trail (supplementary bundle pages 84-91) showing that a document he had described in his witness statement as a purely internal draft response to IPID's fraud and corruption findings against Brigadier Julius Mkhwanazi had in fact been sent, via the City Manager's PA, to the MMC for Community Safety for signature and onward transmission to IPID; Behari ultimately conceded that his statement's account (paragraphs 182-185) was inaccurate. Evidence leader Adv Segeels-Ncube and Commissioners Baloyi SC and Khumalo SC then pressed Behari at length on the substance of that IPID response -- including its claims about Mkhwanazi's authority to accept CAT VIP Protection vehicle donations and register them in the City's name, and about the City's supposed 'benefit' from the transaction -- and on his advice to the City Manager that the fraud and corruption case against Mkhwanazi was 'not sustainable', which the Commissioners suggested effectively blocked disciplinary action despite IPID's directive. The Commission also examined the 22 August 2023 change to the City's disciplinary delegation matrix, which routed referrals through Behari's office in the days following anonymous 'Bhixi-Bhixi' whistleblower emails alleging a clique protecting Mkhwanazi, and around the time Mr Nciza was placed on special leave/suspension. At the close of Behari's testimony, the next witness, Ms Linda Gxasheka, was called and placed on record, but her cross-examination on a newly filed 44-page supplementary statement was postponed to 26 and 27 February 2026.

rulings.description: Cross-examination of the next witness, Ms Linda Gxasheka, postponed to 26 and 27 February 2026 (by agreement between the evidence leader and her legal representative, Adv Magula), given that her 44-page supplementary statement had only been received the previous afternoon; she was directed to attend at 9:30 on both dates and reminded she remains under subpoena, with possible criminal sanction for non-attendance.

summary: Day 55 (6 February 2026) opened with two witnesses excused before testifying: Witness F, whose further testimony was postponed to 16 and 17 February, and Mr Kareem, an implicated person, whose unopposed postponement application -- following late disclosure of a 397-page questioning bundle -- led to a ruling postponing his evidence to 9 and 10 March 2026, with directions to file a witness statement by 27 February and for evidence leaders to furnish supplementary documents by 2 March. The remainder of the day was devoted to continued cross-examination and re-examination of Brigadier Rachel Matjeng regarding her personal relationship with Mr Matlala, director of Medicare 24 (SAPS's medical-surveillance service provider), covering WhatsApp exchanges about disputed non-arrival fee claims, a switch to Signal amid concerns about a 'bugged' phone, requests for Ozempic medication, contact with senior SAPS generals, and disputed payments including an alleged R100,000 and R300,000 routed through a third party's account. summary: SAPS Brigadier Rachel Matjeng, represented by attorney Mr Shirindzi, was sworn in and led through her statement by evidence leader Adv Pooe on her long-running on-and-off romantic relationship with SAPS health risk manager contractor Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala, and on her role overseeing the Medicare 24 Tshwane District medical surveillance contract. Using WhatsApp records extracted from Matlala's phone, Adv Pooe and Commissioners Baloyi SC and Khumalo SC pressed Matjeng on the timeline of her involvement with the contract, her disclosure of the relationship to her supervisor Major General Manamela, and three R100,000 payments from Matlala in January to March 2025 routed through a friend's business account which Matjeng claimed she never actually received. The Chairperson and Commissioners repeatedly characterised aspects of her evidence as implausible or inconsistent with the documentary record, including her explanation for advising Matlala on how to respond to a SAPS non-performance letter and her account of large payments compared to small gifts pre-2024. The hearing adjourned mid-cross-examination and was postponed to continue the following day, 6 February 2026.

The Chairperson found the witness's account of the timing of the Khawula warrant to be untruthful, and Commissioner Baloyi SC separately told the witness his explanation for a R20,000 payment from Matlala was not credible. summary: The Commission first dealt with a second postponement application brought on behalf of Witness F, tied to a pending High Court urgent interdict application; the Chairperson refused it, finding it largely a rehash of a postponement application dismissed the previous week and that its one new argument, a section 35(3) fair-trial/self-incrimination objection, was without merit given that Commission testimony cannot be used in criminal proceedings. The Commission ruled that the evidence leaders could exhibit Witness F's WhatsApp records and comment on them regardless of his stated intention not to participate, and directed that he be put at least four specific questions; Witness F was then sworn in and answered extensive questioning for the remainder of the day. His testimony centred on WhatsApp records showing him relaying messages and favours between Matlala, General Sibiya and others, including arranging delivery of game animals ('impalas') to General Sibiya's private address, receiving and forwarding an unsolicited offer to sell hundreds of shotguns, and repeatedly sharing internal SAPS case and personnel information with civilian contacts.

rulings.description: Witness F's second postponement application was refused; his section 35(3) fair-trial argument was found to be stillborn because evidence given to the Commission cannot be used against a witness in a criminal trial (except for perjury) and the witness retains a privilege against self-incrimination in the proceedings.
Evidence leaders granted leave to present as evidence the WhatsApp chats relating to Witness F, and, as amended, any other evidence (not limited to WhatsApp chats), with commentary as necessary.
Witness F ordered to remain at the remote location from which he was testifying until excused by the Commission.

Evidence leader Adv Chaskalson SC directed to put no fewer than four questions to Witness F, so that a later refusal to answer could properly ground a charge under section 6 of the Commission's Act and Regulation 8(1), rather than allowing the witness a 'free ride' by pre-announcing non-participation.

witnesses.name: Captain Lawrence Itumeleng Makgotloe
witnesses.role_as_described: SAPS Captain and Senior Forensic Analyst in the Automated/Integrated Ballistic Identification System (IBIS) subsection, Forensic Science Laboratory, Pretoria Silverton; formerly a ballistic analyst in the ballistics analysis subsection who processed the Vereeniging crime scene and produced the ballistic report on the Vereeniging and Bramley cases

summary: SAPS ballistic analyst Captain Lawrence Itumeleng Makgotloe testified under oath about processing the 17 April 2024 Vereeniging crime scene, where Mr Armand Swart was shot dead in his vehicle, and the related Bramley arrests, and about the ballistic report he produced linking an AK-47 rifle seized in Bramley to cartridge cases from the murder scene. He acknowledged errors in his report -- an incorrect paragraph cross-reference and a case-number typo -- which he attributed to lab workload and time pressure rather than deliberate manipulation, and said a January-February 2025 quality-management review addressed only the cross-referencing error. Much of his testimony concerned an incident on 7 January 2025 in which he says the investigating officer on the case ("Witness B") and several armed colleagues took him from a police station to the Pretoria forensic lab overnight, interrogated him about the report and about Lt-Col Mangena, and attempted to confiscate his work computer before other SAPS officers intervened -- an episode he has reported to police as a kidnapping, now with IPID. The Chairperson ordered protection of the investigating officers' identities and limited questioning on one further report error to avoid prejudicing a separate, ongoing criminal matter.

rulings.description: Chairperson directed that the names of SAPS investigating-team officers involved in the Vereeniging/Bramley matter not be divulged by the witness, ordering they be referred to by letter (e.g. Witness B) to protect their identities; officers from the witness's own ballistics section were exempted from this order.
Chairperson questioned whether detailed questioning on a firearm serial-number/etching error was necessary, cautioning that it could undermine or damage a separate criminal process still to come.

summary: Day 50 opened with two applications on behalf of a witness due to testify that day: a postponement application, and an application for part of his testimony to be heard without disclosure of his name or image. Attorney Mr Ngoato argued his client had too little time to review a large bundle of WhatsApp chats extracted from his seized cellphones, while evidence leader Adv Chaskalson SC argued the witness had already had adequate notice of the roughly 1,389 pages the Commission intended to focus on. After hearing extensive argument on the timeline of disclosure, the Commission postponed the witness's evidence to Tuesday, 3 February 2026, without ruling on all factual disputes between the parties. The Commission then separately heard and granted the in-camera application, ordering that the witness's testimony be broadcast but that his name and image not be published, on the basis that his physical safety could be at risk.

rulings.description: Postponement granted: the witness's evidence, due to begin 30 January 2026, is postponed to Tuesday, 3 February 2026, on the basis that fairness required the witness be given further time to go through the documentation, rather than the Commission being too exacting about exactly when the documents were received.

summary: Maj-Gen Lesetja Senona concluded his third day of testimony, beginning with an extended procedural dispute over the timing of document disclosure to him and his legal team, which the Commission resolved by continuing the hearing and undertaking to address any specific prejudice as it arose. Evidence leader Adv Hassim SC then took him through further WhatsApp exchanges with Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala concerning a SAPS Medicare24 contract, a meeting Senona helped arrange with then-KZN Police Commissioner General Mkhwanazi, an internal SAPS finance screenshot Senona did not report, and his son's dealings with Matlala over an apartment purchase; Commissioners repeatedly told Senona his answers ('I assumed', 'I do not recall') were evasive. The hearing then replayed a video clip of what appears to be an internal SAPS/Medicare24 meeting about contract non-performance at Senona's request, before turning to his evidence-in-chief on the November 2021 theft of 541kg of cocaine (about R200 million) from the Hawks' Port Shepstone office, where extensive questioning covered inadequate security, prior break-ins, and conflicting officer affidavits about whether patrols had been instructed. The day closed with evidence leader putting to Senona that sharing a confidential 'Nangy' case docket with Matlala breached a SAPS circular on the handling of personal information, after which Senona was excused.

rulings.description: After hearing submissions from the evidence leader, the witness's legal representative and the witness himself on complaints of prejudice from late or piecemeal document disclosure, the Commission ruled to continue with the hearing, noting that where a specific instance of prejudice was raised (as with a video clip shown to the witness overnight before questioning), it would be addressed as it arose rather than halting proceedings generally.

Granted Maj-Gen Senona a short adjournment (about ten minutes) to read a SAPS circular on the handling of personal information that had been handed to him only during the lunch break, before evidence leader resumed questioning him on it.

summary: On Day 48, the Commission opened by finalising a provisional ruling from the previous sitting, directing Major General Lesetja Senona to disclose a name withheld from a WhatsApp text sent to him by Lieutenant-General Mkhwanazi that also referenced General Sibiya, despite safety objections from Senona's legal representative, Ms Mafisa. Evidence leader Adv Hassim SC, assisted by Commissioners Adv Baloyi SC and Adv Khumalo SC, then cross-examined Senona for the full day about his years-long relationship with businessman Vusimusi Matlala, testing his claimed unawareness of extensive contemporaneous media coverage of Matlala's alleged role in the Tembisa Hospital procurement scandal. The Commission also questioned Senona about forwarding Matlala a lengthy police docket containing personal details of a complainant and others, about three documents -- concerning a Mchunu family foundation, material described as relating to President Ramaphosa, and a Rustenburg Municipality corruption report -- that Matlala sent him during an in-person meeting which Senona insisted he never opened, and about advice he gave Matlala after SAPS terminated his company's roughly R360-million contract. The sitting adjourned at 17:00 with Senona's cross-examination unfinished, to resume the next day at 09:30.

summary: The Commission heard two witnesses on the theme of political interference. Maj-Gen Anthony Gopaul testified about two sets of interactions with Minister Senzo Mchunu: repeated calls seeking updates on the 2025 murder investigation of ANC Councillor Mabhida in Mandeni, and a March 2025 episode in which the Minister, campaigning in ANC regalia during the Ward 28 Shakaskraal by-election, summoned station management to explain why an MK party candidate and his sons had not been arrested in various cases. Witness E, testifying under protected-identity arrangements as an undercover Crime Intelligence operative, described being contacted by Minister Mchunu from December 2024 for the names of Crime Intelligence officials he said were involved in planning the 2017 killing of ANC official Sindiso Magaqa, and testified that in December 2025 the Minister dictated the contents of a statement he wanted Witness E to sign implicating Lt-Gen Khumalo, which Witness E said he never drafted.
